title: Population Within Radius: People in the Circle
description: Estimate the population inside a circle with Population Within Radius — census areas apportioned by overlap, method stated. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the tool never pretends a circle is uniform: it sums the census areas your circle actually covers, apportioning each tract or block group by the share of its area inside the line.
quick_answer: Population Within Radius estimates how many people live inside a circle you draw, by adding up the census areas it covers, each apportioned by its overlap with the circle. Set centre and radius and read the estimate with its method attached — the method decides whether the number deserves trust.

body.t: “How many people live within 3 miles?” is the first question of every site decision. The
lists the towns; this tool counts the people.
A new facility's realistic service population, estimated from the census areas it actually covers — the number grant applications ask for by name.
Canvassing, mail drops and event promotion all size themselves by the circle's population before they size their budgets.
How many residents sit within a radius of a site is the first-pass exposure question — estimated honestly here, modelled properly by specialists later.

A 2 km circle at a claimed uniform 5,000 people/km² would hold π × 2² × 5,000 ≈ 62,800 people — but real density is never uniform (a park, a river and a tower block share most circles). The tool's tract-by-tract apportionment exists to replace that fantasy number with a defensible one.

A circle centred on a waterfront spends half its area on the harbour — zero residents, half the circle. Apportionment by land-intersecting census areas handles it; naive area maths counts the fish. Manhattan-edge circles are the classic test.

popular_table.note: Apportionment assumes people spread evenly within each small census area — a good approximation at block-group grain, weaker at tract grain. The figure is an estimate built on the named census, not a headcount.

faq: The smallest areas with published populations that the data supports — block groups where available, tracts otherwise — each apportioned by its land-area overlap with your circle.

As the demographic first pass, yes. Final site decisions deserve current commercial data and a site visit; the circle estimate narrows twenty candidates to three honestly.
The method travels wherever small-area census counts exist; coverage depth varies by country and the tool's data statement names what it holds.
Why not just use density × area?
Because density is not uniform — the uniform-trap example prices the error. Apportionment costs more arithmetic and buys a number you can defend in a meeting.
